items.title: Path Trader
items.description: Self-funded SaaS for Brazilian traders, where I'm the technical co-founder and only engineer, serving about 70 customers. pnpm + Turborepo monorepo with four Next.js 16 apps (web app, marketing site, admin, landing page) and a NestJS 11 API with 56 modules over a 74-model Prisma/PostgreSQL schema. AI assistant with a multi-agent router, tool calling and RAG on pgvector, running on OpenAI or AWS Bedrock with per-plan monthly cost budgets, plus an OAuth-protected MCP server. Asaas subscriptions with idempotent webhooks, pg-boss queues, Pusher, AWS S3/SES, a Serwist PWA, ~500 unit and e2e test files, and 16 GitHub Actions workflows deploying to Vercel and Fly.
items.summary: Self-funded SaaS for Brazilian traders: journaling, analytics, broker imports and an AI assistant with RAG and an MCP server. Technical co-founder and only engineer, now serving about 70 customers.
items.longDescription: Path Trader is an independent, self-funded platform that helps Brazilian traders journal their operations, review performance and manage risk. I co-founded it with a partner who brought the idea and runs marketing; as the only engineer I own the whole technology side, and it now serves about 70 customers. It is a pnpm + Turborepo monorepo with four Next.js 16 apps (the web app, the marketing site, the admin panel and a landing page) and a NestJS 11 API, sharing eleven internal packages and one Prisma schema of 74 models on PostgreSQL across 56 API modules. Trades come in through eight broker-specific import parsers (MetaTrader 4/5, Profit, TradingView and others). The AI assistant is a multi-agent chat router with tool calling and retrieval over a pgvector corpus; it runs on OpenAI or AWS Bedrock behind a provider abstraction, prices every request from its tokens, and enforces a monthly cost budget per plan. An OAuth-protected MCP server lets traders query their own journal from Claude and other MCP clients. Billing runs on Asaas subscriptions: webhooks are authenticated and processed asynchronously by idempotent handlers, a daily job reconciles missed events, and service invoices (NFS-e) are issued automatically. Long-running work such as AI turns, imports and notifications goes through pg-boss queues on Postgres, with realtime updates over Pusher and storage and email on AWS S3/SES. The web app is a Serwist PWA, the API is hardened with helmet and global rate limiting, Sentry covers the API and public apps, and about 500 Jest and Playwright test files run across 16 GitHub Actions workflows that release and deploy to Vercel and Fly.
highlights: pnpm + Turborepo monorepo: four Next.js 16 apps and a NestJS 11 API (56 modules) sharing 11 packages and a 74-model Prisma schema
AI assistant: multi-agent router with tool calling and RAG on pgvector, on OpenAI or AWS Bedrock, with per-plan monthly cost budgets
OAuth-protected MCP server so traders can use their journal from Claude and other MCP clients
Asaas billing with authenticated, idempotent webhook handlers, daily reconciliation and automatic NFS-e invoices
Eight broker import parsers and pg-boss queues for AI turns, imports and notifications, with Pusher realtime and AWS S3/SES
~500 Jest and Playwright test files and 16 GitHub Actions workflows: tests, e2e suites, automated releases, backups and deploys to Vercel and Fly

caseStudy.problem: Brazilian traders journal their trades in spreadsheets, if at all, so they can't see their own patterns: which setups pay, when they overtrade, how much risk they really take. Path Trader turns imported trades into a journal and analytics, with an AI assistant that answers questions over the trader's own data.

hardPart.title: Billing that never loses an event
hardPart.text: Subscriptions run on Asaas, and a payment webhook that is dropped or delivered twice means a customer loses access or gets charged wrong. Webhooks are authenticated and processed asynchronously by idempotent handlers, so a retry is a no-op; a daily job reconciles with Asaas to catch anything missed, and service invoices (NFS-e) are issued automatically. The AI assistant gets the same care on cost: every request is priced from its tokens and checked against a monthly budget per plan.

caseStudy.result: About 70 customers, 540 merged pull requests and about 56 production deployments, each gated by GitHub Actions running type checks, unit and end-to-end tests. Built and run as the only engineer and technical co-founder; my partner brought the idea and runs marketing.

architecture.note: Sentry across the API and public apps · 16 GitHub Actions workflows deploy to Vercel and Fly

items.title: Bird · No-code dashboard builder
items.description: No-code analytics dashboard builder I architected at Bird, an Amsterdam-based cloud communications platform. Users compose queries field by field on Malloy and render them with Vega as line, bar, doughnut and funnel charts, tables or KPIs, on a drag-and-drop layout with inline edit, clone and delete. SolidJS UI with TanStack Query as the server-state layer, shipped dark behind organization-scoped feature flags and used in production by enterprise customers on datasets of 1M+ records.
items.summary: Analytics where customers pick their own metrics: compose a query field by field, render it as a chart, table or KPI, arrange it by drag and drop. In production for enterprise customers on datasets of 1M+ records.
items.longDescription: Bird is an Amsterdam-based cloud communications platform (SMS, WhatsApp, email, marketing and sales). In its analytics product I architected the no-code dashboard builder. Users compose a query by adding and removing fields, then render it as a line, bar, doughnut or funnel chart, a table or a KPI. Widgets sit on a drag-and-drop layout and can be edited inline, cloned or deleted. Every widget is a Malloy query whose result feeds a Vega spec; the UI is SolidJS, with TanStack Query as the server-state layer. All of it went to production dark behind organization-scoped feature flags, was tested in our own workspace and then rolled out gradually, covered by Vitest, React Testing Library and Playwright. Bird's UI is under NDA, so this page shows the architecture instead of screenshots.
highlights: Field-by-field query composition on Malloy: users add and remove fields instead of writing queries or filing a request with engineering
One rendering path from a Malloy result to a Vega spec, covering line, bar, doughnut and funnel charts, tables and KPIs
Drag-and-drop layout with inline edit, clone and delete for every widget
TanStack Query as the server-state layer, caching and deduplicating widget queries
Shipped dark behind organization-scoped feature flags and rolled out gradually, with Vitest, React Testing Library and Playwright coverage

caseStudy.problem: Bird's customers wanted analytics on their own data, and every new chart meant a request to engineering. The answer had to be self-serve, and it had to stay usable for enterprise accounts whose datasets run past 1M records.

hardPart.title: Staying interactive on 1M+ records
hardPart.text: The builder never ships raw rows to the browser. Each widget is a Malloy query, so filtering and aggregation run in the database and the client only receives the small result set a chart, table or KPI needs. TanStack Query sits between the widgets and the API as the server-state layer: results are cached per query, so rearranging the layout does not refetch what is already on screen.

caseStudy.result: In production for enterprise customers on datasets of 1M+ records. Customers build the dashboard they need without waiting on an engineer, and every release reached them gradually behind feature flags.

architecture.note: SolidJS UI · shipped dark behind organization-scoped feature flags

items.title: Tavi
items.description: AI-first personal assistant for daily life: log water, meals, workouts, weight, tasks and money by talking to it, in the app or from Claude through MCP. The marketing site is live at oitavi.com.br and the API runs in production on AWS; the iOS and Android apps are not in the stores yet. Offline-first React Native app (Expo SDK 58) on local SQLite synced to Postgres through self-hosted PowerSync, native home screen widgets, a NestJS 12 API with a streamed Claude agent that confirms every change on screen, an MCP server behind its own OAuth 2.1, finances kept only on the phone, infrastructure as AWS CDK and a Next.js site built for search and AI answer engines.
items.summary: Talk to it from Claude or ChatGPT: an AI-first personal assistant with its own MCP server. Log water, meals, workouts, tasks and money by talking, in an offline-first app or from your AI. Site live, API on AWS, apps not in the stores yet.
items.longDescription: Tavi (formerly Pocket Helper) is a personal assistant for daily life: water, meals, workouts, weight, task lists and personal finances, logged by just saying "drank 500 ml, did 5 rounds of pads, weigh 84.2". The website is live at oitavi.com.br and the backend is in production, while the iOS and Android apps are still on their way to the stores. The core app is plain, fast CRUD that works without AI; the assistant is a layer on top. The mobile app is React Native on Expo SDK 58 and it is offline-first: every screen reads a local SQLite database that syncs with Postgres through a self-hosted PowerSync service, and devices write through one upload endpoint with an allow-list of tables and columns, ownership checks and a savepoint per operation, so a bad write is refused without blocking the device's queue. Native home screen widgets (SwiftUI on iOS, RemoteViews on Android, through a local Expo module) show the day from a snapshot the app writes: water against the goal with a +250 ml button, the next tasks to tick off and, during a workout, the rest timer with the same buttons as the live notification and iOS Live Activity. Presses are queued natively and work with the app closed. The NestJS 12 API on Drizzle and Postgres 18 runs the assistant on Claude Haiku 5.5: replies stream over server-sent events with the thinking summary and each tool step, and every change the agent proposes is rehearsed by the sync engine in a rolled-back transaction and shown as a confirmation card built from the real rows. One set of Zod schemas defines the API validation and the tools, so Claude, ChatGPT and other assistants get the same read, add and confirmed-change tools through an MCP server, behind an OAuth 2.1 authorization server written into the API, with app and MCP confirmations kept on separate channels. Finances never reach the backend: they live in a per-user SQLCipher database on the phone with automatic, password-encrypted Google Drive backups. Production runs on one EC2 instance in São Paulo defined in AWS CDK: Caddy, the API, Postgres and PowerSync in Docker, no SSH (Session Manager only), no NAT gateway, a separate data disk with daily snapshots, secrets in Parameter Store, and a deploy script that builds the ARM image, pushes it to ECR and restarts the stack. The marketing site is Next.js 16 with Tailwind 4 and Motion, in Portuguese and English, styled from the app's own design tokens and built to be found by search engines and AI answer engines: JSON-LD, hreflang, an Open Graph image per page and language, llms.txt and IndexNow. Pro subscriptions go through RevenueCat, and AI costs are capped per user and globally before each call.
highlights: Website live at oitavi.com.br: Next.js 16, Tailwind 4 and Motion, pt-BR and English, built from the app's design tokens, with JSON-LD, per-page Open Graph images, llms.txt and IndexNow for search and AI answer engines

Production on AWS defined in CDK: one EC2 instance running Caddy, the API, Postgres 18 and PowerSync in Docker, no SSH or NAT gateway, a separate data disk with daily snapshots and secrets in Parameter Store
Offline-first React Native (Expo SDK 58) on local SQLite, synced to Postgres through self-hosted PowerSync with an allow-listed upload contract and per-operation savepoints
Native home screen widgets on iOS and Android: water, tasks to tick off and the live workout's rest timer, with presses queued natively so they work with the app closed

Claude agent with streamed replies and tool steps; every change is dry-run by the sync engine and confirmed on a card, and the same tools reach Claude and ChatGPT through an MCP server behind OAuth 2.1
Finances stay on the phone in a per-user SQLCipher database with automatic, password-encrypted Google Drive backups; RevenueCat subscriptions and AI cost limits checked before every call

items.title: Bem Coberto
items.description: Brazilian travel insurance marketplace in development: one search quotes several insurers in parallel, every plan is normalized into one comparable format, and the customer pays with Pix or card. Strict TypeScript monorepo (pnpm + Turborepo) with a Next.js App Router web app, a NestJS API on Fastify, insurer adapters behind one TravelInsuranceProvider interface, a transactional outbox with a BullMQ worker for issuing, PostgreSQL, Redis and AWS.
items.summary: Travel insurance marketplace for Brazilian travellers: quote several insurers in one search, compare every plan in one format, pay with Pix or card. Built around insurer adapters, a payment-safe order state machine and an outbox-driven worker.
items.longDescription: Bem Coberto is a travel insurance marketplace for Brazilian travellers, currently in development. One search quotes several insurers in parallel, every plan is normalized into one comparable format, and the customer pays with Pix or card and receives the policy by email and in their account. The hard part is money and policies moving between systems that share no transactions, so the architecture is built around a few firm rules. Each insurer sits behind a single TravelInsuranceProvider adapter (quote, issue, find issued, cancel, health): domain code never sees an insurer's types, and adding an insurer means writing one adapter. Quotes fan out with per-insurer timeouts, are cached in Redis, and degrade to partial results when one insurer fails. Payment follows a charge-then-issue model: the payment webhook marks the order paid and writes an outbox row in the same database transaction, and a BullMQ worker issues the policy, stores the files and sends the email. Orders move through an explicit state machine owned by the domain package, every transition is recorded, and an issue call that times out is never retried blindly; it is reconciled against the insurer, so no one is charged without a policy or a refund. The stack is a strict TypeScript monorepo on pnpm and Turborepo: Next.js App Router for the storefront and back office, NestJS on Fastify for the API, PostgreSQL with Prisma, Redis, S3 and SES on AWS, with every decision recorded in a build spec and ADRs.
highlights: Insurer adapters behind one TravelInsuranceProvider interface: domain code never imports an insurer's types, and adding an insurer never touches checkout
Parallel quoting with per-insurer timeouts, Redis caching and partial results when an insurer is down, targeting under 8 s at p95
Payment-safe issuing: transactional outbox, BullMQ worker, and reconciliation instead of blind retries, so no one is charged without a policy or a refund
Order state machine in a pure domain package, alongside integer-cent money, Pix and card pricing with installments, and a best-value ranking that checks the Schengen €30k minimum
One Zod contract shared by API and web: requests validated, every response parsed at runtime, OpenAPI 3.1 generated from the same schemas
Quality gates in CI: lint, typecheck, Vitest, Playwright end-to-end tests with axe accessibility checks, and a 200 KB JavaScript budget on results

items.title: Vestra Financial Management
items.description: Mobile-first personal finance PWA built as a pnpm + Turborepo monorepo: a Vite + React 19 dashboard with a Workbox service worker, a Next.js 16 marketing site, and a NestJS 11 API on Prisma and PostgreSQL (17 models, money stored as Decimal). Global JWT auth with refresh-token rotation, workspace owner/member guards, transactional workspace cloning, scheduled recurring transactions, Pusher and Web Push notifications, and free/pro plan limits. Deployed on Fly.io and Vercel with Neon Postgres.
items.summary: Mobile-first PWA for personal finance: shared workspaces with owner/member roles, recurring transactions and push reminders. Turborepo with a React 19 dashboard, a Next.js site and a NestJS API.
items.longDescription: Vestra is a mobile-first PWA for personal finance where several people can share a workspace. It is a pnpm + Turborepo monorepo with three apps and four shared packages: a Vite + React 19 dashboard installed as a PWA through a custom Workbox service worker, a Next.js 16 marketing site, and a NestJS 11 API on Prisma and PostgreSQL. The API is split into 14 domain modules over a 17-model schema, with money stored as Decimal rather than floats. Authentication is global by default: a JWT guard protects every route unless it is explicitly marked public, refresh tokens rotate on every use in an httpOnly cookie, and workspace owner/member guards enforce who can see and change what. Workspaces can be deep-cloned in a single database transaction that remaps every foreign key. A scheduled job generates recurring transactions and payment reminders, delivered in real time through Pusher and as Web Push notifications with per-user deduplication. Free and pro plans are enforced on the server. Both frontends share a shadcn-style component library on Tailwind 4, and the stack runs on Fly.io and Vercel with Neon Postgres, applying migrations on release with rolling deploys.
highlights: pnpm + Turborepo monorepo: React 19 dashboard, Next.js 16 site and NestJS 11 API sharing UI, types and lint/tsconfig packages
Secure by default: a global JWT guard with an explicit public opt-out, refresh-token rotation in httpOnly cookies, and workspace owner/member guards
Workspace deep clone in one database transaction that remaps every foreign key
17-model Prisma schema on PostgreSQL, with money stored as Decimal, never floats
Scheduled recurring transactions and payment reminders, delivered through Pusher and Web Push with per-user deduplication
Installable PWA (Workbox service worker) on Vercel, API on Fly.io with release-time migrations, rolling deploys and Neon Postgres

items.title: Park the Cart
items.description: Free 3D browser game: push a shopping cart with one bad wheel across a crowded supermarket car park and into the corral without scratching the cars, and every scratch goes on the receipt. No physics engine and no 3D library: the cart is a hand-written rigid-body model in a deterministic core with its own trig functions, so a replay link is just the inputs and a messy 40-second run ends bit-identical in Chromium, Firefox, WebKit and Node. A parking bot plans with A* and drives the real simulation, so all ten levels and every day's daily level are proven finishable, and CI replays forty bot runs. The car park is drawn by about 2,300 lines of hand-written WebGL 2, with models built in code and real shadows.
items.summary: A 3D browser game: park a shopping cart with one bad wheel without scratching the cars. Hand-written cart physics and WebGL 2, replays that are bit-identical across browsers, and a bot that proves every level can be finished.
items.longDescription: Park the Cart (Estacione o Carrinho) is a free, open source 3D browser game, in English and Portuguese, on desktop and phone: push a shopping cart with one bad wheel across a crowded supermarket car park and into the corral without scratching the cars. Every scratch goes on the receipt, each level has a card limit that starts at R$ 4,000 and ends at R$ 100, and the result is a receipt like "R$ 3,480 of damage in 41 seconds". There are ten levels, a daily level that is the same for everyone, five carts and replays you can share as a link. The game is a pure function of the level, the cart and the player's inputs. There is no physics engine: the cart is a rigid body on four wheels in about 200 lines, with fixed rear wheels that cancel sideways slip, swivelling front casters and one faulty caster that alternates stuck and rolling phases drawn from the level's seed. Since nobody can feel a slider in a test suite, the feel is pinned by measurements (drift per second, top speed, coasting and braking distance, sliding in the rain) and a property test checks that no cart ever gains energy without input. A replay link is only the inputs, run-length encoded as varints in base64url, so the same inputs must give the same run in every browser: a fixed 120 Hz step and quantised inputs handle most of it, and because Math.sin, cos and atan2 differ between V8, SpiderMonkey and JavaScriptCore, the core has its own trig built only from exactly rounded operations, with an ESLint rule that bans the others, Math.random and the clock in the core. An end-to-end test plays a messy 40-second run in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit and checks that the final state is bit-identical to Node's. A parking bot plans a path with A* on a 25 cm grid around everything that can bill, then drives the real simulation with a steering and speed controller, waiting for gaps in moving traffic. Levels are generated from a spec and a seed and kept only if the bot parks them with R$ 0 of damage; the bot's run ships as the level's par, CI replays forty bot runs across the carts, and the daily level re-rolls until the bot can finish it, so over 2,000 simulated days every one was finishable. The car park is 3D without a 3D library: about 2,300 lines of WebGL 2 written for the game, with cars, carts, cones and kerbs built in code from the same sizes the collisions use, painted asphalt, one low sun with a shadow map that falls through the baskets' wire mesh, and a flat top-down renderer as the fallback. The matrices, camera and models are plain functions unit tested in Node, and the bundle is held under a 200 KB budget.
highlights: Hand-written cart model with no physics engine: fixed rear wheels, swivelling casters and one faulty wheel, with the feel pinned by measurements and a no-free-energy property test
Deterministic core with its own trig built from exactly rounded operations, so a 40-second run ends bit-identical in Chromium, Firefox, WebKit and Node
Replays shared as a link: run-length-encoded inputs as varints in base64url, parsed strictly as untrusted input and fuzzed with fast-check
A parking bot with A* and a driving controller proves every level finishable; CI replays forty bot runs, and the daily level re-rolls until the bot parks it
3D without a 3D library: about 2,300 lines of WebGL 2, models built in code from the collision sizes, a shadow map and a flat renderer as fallback
Ten levels, a daily level, five carts, English and Portuguese, desktop and phone, under a 200 KB bundle budget

items.title: The Single Hole
items.description: Free multiplayer browser game where everyone on the internet digs the same hole, from Brazil to Japan, with a spoon: one shared depth, live, no login. The real problem is the number: thousands of clients adding to one counter in real time with optimistic updates, reconciliation, server-side rate limits and persistence. The room is pure logic with a fake clock, run in production as a Cloudflare Worker with one Durable Object on the WebSocket Hibernation API. Load tested at 6,000 players digging with 34 ms p95 broadcast latency. three.js with procedural textures, ~175 KB of initial JS.
items.summary: Everyone on the internet digs the same hole, live, from Brazil to Japan with a spoon. One shared counter for thousands of clients on a Cloudflare Durable Object, load tested at 6,000 players and 34 ms p95.
items.longDescription: The Single Hole (Um Buraco Só) is a free, open source browser game played from a link with no login: everyone digs the same hole, from a backyard in Brazil to a rock garden in Kyoto, with a spoon. Each player is a spoon on the rim, tagged with their country and scoop count; a cross-section shows the eight layers down to the core, and a globe shows who is digging right now and the year we reach Japan at this week's pace. The interesting problem is the number: thousands of clients adding to one shared counter in real time. The room is a single authoritative class with no timers, sockets or storage: connections, raw messages and the clock go in, messages come out, so every rule is unit tested with a fake clock and hosting is a thin adapter, a Node WebSocket server for development and a Cloudflare Worker with one Durable Object in production. The client applies your scoops at once, batches them every 400 ms through a mirror of the server's token bucket, and eases the display toward the server's total plus your unconfirmed scoops without ever going backwards; batches in flight when the connection drops are discarded rather than risk counting twice. Every message is validated before the room sees it, with per-connection and per-IP scoop limits, connection caps, strikes for bad input and a first-come line once the room holds 10,000 players; the country comes from platform headers, never from the client. State is snapshotted every few seconds with a backup copy, and the room refuses to start rather than silently reset a live hole to zero. On Cloudflare it uses the WebSocket Hibernation API, so it costs almost nothing while idle. One room held 6,000 players digging at 34 ms p95 broadcast latency and reached its 10,000-player cap at 55 ms p95. Rendering is three.js with procedural textures and no image assets, with a lazy-loaded globe and ~175 KB of initial JS checked against a budget in CI. No accounts, names or cookies; IPs live only in memory for rate limits.
highlights: One authoritative room as pure logic (no timers, sockets or storage), unit tested with a fake clock, behind Node and Cloudflare Durable Object adapters
Optimistic client: batches every 400 ms through a mirror of the server's token bucket, and a display that reconciles to the server total without going backwards
Load tested at 6,000 players digging with 34 ms p95 broadcast latency, and 55 ms p95 at the 10,000-player cap, with a waiting line past it
Abuse handling: validated protocol, per-connection and per-IP rate limits, strikes, and country from platform headers, covered by abuse tests
Snapshots with a backup copy, a room that refuses to start rather than reset to zero, and WebSocket Hibernation so it is cheap when idle
three.js with procedural textures and no image assets, a lazy-loaded globe and ~175 KB of initial JS under a CI budget

items.title: Cartório Simulator
items.description: Free daily browser game: get one document stamped at a Brazilian cartório before the windows close for lunch. Each day's bureaucracy is generated from a seed and is the same for everyone. The game is a pure function of a seed and the player's inputs: a seeded generator builds a dependency graph of documents that is solvable by construction, property tests run a solver over 10,000 days to check a fairness bound, and windows, queues and the 30× clock are deterministic state machines, so a bug report is a seed plus an input log. The forms are real HTML form controls, playable by keyboard and screen reader.
items.summary: A daily browser game about Brazilian bureaucracy: get one stamp before lunch. Every day's chain is generated from a seed, solvable by construction, and checked by a solver over 10,000 days in the test suite.
items.longDescription: Cartório Simulator is a free daily browser game, in English and Portuguese, on desktop and phone: get one document stamped at a Brazilian cartório before the windows close for lunch. Window 3 says you need Form 27-B, Form 27-B needs a copy, the copy must be authenticated at Window 4, and Window 4 goes to lunch in 40 seconds. You take a ticket, queue, fill in forms where every form has a trap, get sent back and try again, then paste your result: time, forms, send-backs and your path through the windows. The game is a pure function of a seed and the player's inputs. A seeded generator builds a dependency graph of documents backwards from the day's goal, so every chain is solvable by construction. A discovery solver that plays like a careful first-time player runs over 10,000 consecutive days plus 500 random seeds on every test run and checks that each one finishes within a 6-minute fairness bound; the seed report puts the median at 1:18. Windows, queues, lunch breaks and the 30× cartório clock are state machines advanced in fixed ticks, so the run saved in localStorage is just a list of ticks and actions, and replaying it rebuilds the exact state: a bug report is a date plus that log. The hall is drawn on a canvas, and the paper (forms, ticket, folder, stamps) is real HTML form controls, playable with a keyboard and a screen reader and readable on a phone. Pure game logic lives in its own folder with no DOM, the bundle is held under 200 KB by the check script, and GitHub Actions runs the checks and a Playwright smoke test on every push and deploys to GitHub Pages.
highlights: The whole game is a pure function of a seed and the player's inputs: a run is replayed exactly from an input log
Seeded generator that builds a document dependency graph backwards from the goal, solvable by construction
Property tests run a solver over 10,000 consecutive days plus 500 random seeds and enforce a 6-minute fairness bound
Windows, queues, lunch breaks and a 30× clock as state machines advanced in fixed ticks
Forms are real HTML form controls, playable by keyboard and screen reader, in English and Portuguese
Bundle held under 200 KB, Playwright smoke test and deploy to GitHub Pages on every push

items.title: My Links
items.description: Self-hosted link-in-bio page: one static page with my photo, a short bio and my links, in English and Portuguese, driven by a single JSON file. The build is the validator: a strict Zod schema stops the build on a misspelt key, a javascript: URL or a missing image, so a typo made on GitHub fails CI and never reaches the live page. A Next.js static export with only two small client islands, accessible by default with axe in CI, a strict Content Security Policy, no cookies or analytics, and Lighthouse 95 / 100 / 100 / 100 on mobile.
items.summary: My link-in-bio page, self-hosted: one static page driven by one JSON file that the build validates. Next.js static export, two client islands, axe in CI and a strict CSP.
items.longDescription: My Links is the page behind the link in my bios: my photo, a short bio, social icons, links as cards, section headings and one featured project card, in English at / and Portuguese at /pt/. It replaces a hosted link-in-bio service with a page I own, and everything on it comes from one file, content/links.json. That file is parsed with a strict Zod schema when the page is built, so a misspelt key, a title that is too long, an image that is not in public/ or an unsafe URL stops the build with a message that points at the field; links accept only https:, mailto: and paths on the site, and javascript:, data:, http:, protocol-relative URLs and paths with whitespace or .. are rejected and tested. Editing the links on GitHub is enough: CI validates the file and Vercel builds and deploys it. It is a Next.js App Router static export: the profile, cards and footer are Server Components rendered to HTML at build time, and the share dialog and a scroll reveal are the only client components, so the page renders and animates without JavaScript. The share dialog shares the whole page or a single link by copy, WhatsApp, LinkedIn, X, e-mail or the phone's own share sheet. Each language is its own static page with its own html lang, metadata, hreflang links and Open Graph image, all generated from the same file. Accessibility is built in: real links and buttons, a native dialog that moves focus in and back, 44 px touch targets, reduced motion respected, and text contrast checked by a unit test for every colour pairing, with axe running in CI on the page and the open dialog on desktop and phone. vercel.json sets a strict Content Security Policy, HSTS and the other security headers, and the local preview server applies the same file, so the end-to-end tests run under the real CSP and fail on any console error. There are no cookies, analytics or requests to other origins. On mobile Lighthouse scores 95 / 100 / 100 / 100, and a size check fails CI if first-load JS goes over 150 KB gzipped.
highlights: One JSON file drives the page, and the build is the validator: a strict Zod schema fails CI on a bad key, an unsafe URL or a missing image, pointing at the field
Next.js static export with Server Components and only two client islands; the page renders and animates without JavaScript
Share dialog for the page and each link: copy, WhatsApp, LinkedIn, X, e-mail and the native share sheet, with share URLs covered by property tests
English and Portuguese as separate static pages, each with its own lang, metadata, hreflang and Open Graph image
Accessible by default: native dialog focus handling, 44 px targets, reduced motion, a contrast test for every colour pair and axe in CI on desktop and phone
Strict CSP and security headers tested end to end, no cookies or analytics, Lighthouse 95 / 100 / 100 / 100 and a 150 KB JS budget in CI

items.title: Dig to Japan with a Spoon
items.description: Absurd 3D game for Steam, in development: dig from a Brazilian backyard to a family's kitchen in Japan with a teaspoon, then dig back home with chopsticks, with a third-person camera inside the hole. A 3D remake of my own 2D version in Godot 4: the game logic, content and tests were carried over unchanged and only the views were rebuilt, so 768 GUT tests in GitHub Actions prove it still plays like the original. Every model is built from primitives in code, and the store screenshots, Steam capsules, trailer and shorts are rendered from the game itself.
items.summary: A 3D Godot game for Steam: dig from Brazil to Japan with a spoon, then back with chopsticks, from inside the hole. Rebuilt from my 2D version with the logic and tests kept intact, and every model built in code.
items.longDescription: Dig to Japan with a Spoon (Cavar até o Japão com uma Colher) is a short, deliberately silly single-player game for Steam, currently in development and playable start to finish. A guy in a Brazilian backyard digs to Japan with a teaspoon, through every layer of the Earth, while a mole in sunglasses judges him and the neighbour films it for the street's group chat; the second game is the trip back with chopsticks. It started as a 2D game, and this is its 3D remake in Godot 4 with GDScript, with a third-person camera inside the shaft that you orbit to find treasures in the walls. The 2D game stays the source of truth: its game logic (dig state, progression, shop, saves, achievements), its content as Godot resources and its logic tests were ported unchanged, and only the views were rebuilt, so if the ported tests pass and the balance simulator's report matches, the 3D game plays like the 2D one. 768 GUT tests run headless in GitHub Actions on every push, against a SHA-512-verified Godot binary. Depth is still just a number: the shaft is a short tube of wall that scrolls and changes its shader material per layer, with fog and a real lamp on the helmet, so deeper means darker for free. There are no imported meshes: the Digger, the cast, the props, the tools and the treasures are built from rounded primitives in code, in a soft vinyl toy style with expressive faces. The set pieces are scripted in 3D, from a cut-open Earth for the zoom-out gag to chopsticks that hold rocks as physics bodies that really drop. The store screenshots, Steam capsules in every size, a dubbed trailer and vertical shorts are staged and rendered from the game by scripts, and a scripted dive through both games produces a performance report. Windows, Linux and macOS builds are exported with GodotSteam for achievements and rich presence; what is left is playtesting, a Steam Deck check and the launch.
highlights: 3D remake of my 2D game in Godot 4: logic, content and tests carried over unchanged and only the views rebuilt, so the ported tests and balance report prove it plays the same
768 GUT tests running headless in GitHub Actions on every push, against a SHA-512-verified Godot binary
Every model built from rounded primitives in code, in a soft vinyl toy style, with no imported meshes
Third-person camera inside a looping shaft whose shader material changes per layer, with fog and a real helmet lamp
Scripted 3D set pieces: a cut-open Earth for the zoom-out gag and chopsticks that hold rocks as physics bodies
Store screenshots, Steam capsules, a dubbed trailer and shorts rendered from the game by scripts; Windows, Linux and macOS builds with GodotSteam

items.title: Shave the Capybara
items.description: Silly 3D game for Steam, in development: climb a sleeping, neighbourhood-sized capybara and shave her to 100% with one disposable razor without waking her up, then glue it all back on in the second game. Built in Godot 4: you walk on her curved body with gravity toward her surface, her parts are generated ellipsoid meshes whose UVs are the shave grid, and the fur mixes instanced tufts near the camera with a shell shader further away, both thinned by the shave mask. Data-driven content, 365 GUT tests in CI including a full-playthrough test, and a balance simulator holding the pacing at about 5 hours plus 2.
items.summary: A 3D Godot game for Steam: shave a giant sleeping capybara without waking her, then glue the fur back on. Walking on a curved body, fur that reacts to every pass of the razor, and 365 tests in CI.
items.longDescription: Shave the Capybara (Raspa a Capivara) is the follow-up to Dig to Japan with a Spoon, a single-player 3D game for Steam currently in development. A capybara the size of a neighbourhood is asleep in the Pantanal, and a retired barber bet his whole town he could shave her with one disposable razor. You climb her and shave her strip by strip across eight body zones, dealing with knots, burrs, a tick village with a mayor and an election, twelve animal guests to relocate and a dark ear cave, while keeping her asleep with lullabies and managing the razor's edge, skin irritation and the cold. When she wakes up bald, the second game is gluing it all back on. It is built in Godot 4 with GDScript, with the same architecture as Dig to Japan: game logic in scripts with no rendering, unit tested with GUT, and content as Godot resources (8 zones, 20 problems, 6 razors, 40 lost items, 6 lullabies, 38 achievements). Walking on her is pure vector math in a testable SurfaceWalker: gravity points into her surface and the camera's heading is carried from one "up" to the next without spinning. Her body is built from ellipsoid meshes generated in code whose UVs are the shave grid's coordinates, so the shave mask texture maps straight onto her. The fur combines MultiMesh tufts near the camera with a shell shader for the soft look further away, both driven by that mask, with a quality setting, a benchmark tool and incremental rebuilds that only touch what the razor changed. 365 tests run in GitHub Actions on every push, including a full-playthrough test that proves every problem can be solved, every collectible reached and both endings unlocked, and a balance simulator that holds the main game at about 5 hours and the second at about 2. It is ready for the Steam Deck by design: it pauses when the window loses focus or a controller disconnects, saves and settings are written atomically, and a test keeps all text at 14 px or more at Deck resolution. Windows, Linux and macOS builds, GodotSteam achievements, store screenshots, a trailer and shorts are already done.
highlights: Walking on a giant curved body: gravity toward her surface and a camera heading carried between "up" directions, as pure, unit-tested math
Body built from ellipsoid meshes generated in code whose UVs are the shave grid, so the shave mask maps straight onto her
Fur that mixes MultiMesh tufts near the camera with a shell shader further away, thinned by the shave mask, with quality settings and incremental rebuilds
365 GUT tests in GitHub Actions, including a full-playthrough test that proves every problem is solvable and both endings are reachable
Data-driven content (8 zones, 20 problems, 40 lost items, 38 achievements) and a balance simulator holding the pacing at about 5 hours plus 2
Steam Deck readiness: pause on focus loss and controller disconnect, atomic saves and a 14 px text floor test; Windows, Linux and macOS builds with GodotSteam
